sections.h2: How a Mt. Lebanon sale works
sections.html:
A Mt. Lebanon sale follows the usual Pennsylvania routes: list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or take a cash offer. A few municipal and county steps sit on top. Mt. Lebanon is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, roughly four to six miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, and its Inspection Office, tax office and county records all affect the closing date.

Line up the local pieces first, from open permits to the 2026 tax rates and the county appeal calendar.

Most houses here are early twentieth century commuter homes. The first streetcar line to Pittsburgh opened on July 1, 1901, the Liberty Tubes followed in 1924, and the population jumped from 2,258 in 1920 to 13,403 in 1930. About 4,400 properties sit inside a National Register historic district established in 2014, with Foursquare, Tudor, Colonial Revival, Bungalow and Dutch Colonial styles all common.

Age shows up when a buyer inspects roofs, windows, porches, masonry and basement drainage. The municipality offers an illustrated design guide for historic homes and a contractor vetting guide, which helps you decide whether to renovate before listing or sell without touching it.

Typical value of an owned home in Mount Lebanon township for 2020 to 2024 is $378,300, with 72.3 percent of units occupied by owners across 13,646 households. Median household income over the same period was $123,771.

sections.h2: Permits and inspections that can delay a closing
sections.html:
Open building permits are the most common local snag, because the Inspection Office withholds lien letters while permits are open. If you finished a deck, remodel, furnace swap or fence, confirm every final inspection is on record before you set a settlement date.

  • Work started without a permit can draw fines set by the magisterial district judge, so ask the Inspection Office how to regularize it.
  • Residential building permits generally issue within 15 business days, while zoning permits for items such as an air conditioning unit, driveway, fence or shed take up to 30 days.
  • Fences in single-family districts may reach six feet in side and rear yards, are not allowed in front yards, and cannot be solid.
  • A front porch may extend no more than 10 feet into the front yard, and new or replaced front stairs need a building permit.
  • Every private swimming pool carries an annual operation permit and a safety inspection.

On the first Wednesday of each month the office holds Inspections Consultations from 2 to 5 p.m. Appointments last 30 minutes and require preregistering at 412-343-3408.

An ordinary resale doesn't call for a Certificate of Occupancy, which covers changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction. Call the same number to confirm anything specific to your address.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and rates
sections.html:
A Mt. Lebanon parcel carried a combined 42.963 mills in 2026, divided among the municipality, the school district and Allegheny County. The municipal tax office, on the ground floor of the municipal building, collects real estate tax for both the municipality and the Mt. Lebanon School District.

2026 real estate millage on a Mt. Lebanon parcel
Taxing bodyMills
Mt. Lebanon Municipality4.50
Mt. Lebanon School District32.033
Allegheny County6.43
Combined42.963

Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount period through July 31, a face period from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty after that. The school portion can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28. Unpaid balances move to private delinquent collectors each March.

The tax office can supply a bill or receipt, and a title company will usually ask for one before closing. For address changes, the Allegheny County Treasurer handles the request.

Allegheny County assesses every Mt. Lebanon parcel on a 2012 base year, and the last county-wide reassessment took place in 2013. The county office may change a value only for omissions, mathematical or clerical errors, physical changes such as demolitions or building permits, and the occasional interim request from a school district or municipality.

The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears challenges. The annual window runs from July 1 through September 1, and the board mails residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead. It applies a common level ratio to the market value in appeals, and that ratio is 49.3 percent for the 2027 tax year. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal.

A catastrophic loss such as a fire allows a reduction request within six months of the event. Under Act 29 of 2026, buyers of non-owner-occupied property must send contact details to the chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a false filing can bring a fine up to $500. If your buyer is an investor, remind them.

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax starts at 1 percent of the value transferred, and Allegheny County adds municipal and school district shares so the total ranges from 2 to 5 percent across the county. The county Department of Real Estate collects both the state and local portions at recording, and the tax goes on a separate check from the recording fees.

A 2 percent total splits into 1 percent to the state, half a percent to the township and half a percent to the school district. Call the Department of Real Estate for the rate that covers Mt. Lebanon and its school district, since the local share is set by those bodies.

Some family transfers are exempt, and a Statement of Value (form REV-183) is required when the deed lists no consideration or claims an exemption. Grantor and grantee are jointly liable, so the settlement statement should show who pays.

Buyers tend to focus on walkable blocks near Uptown, which runs along Washington Road (U.S. Route 19 Truck) and holds 182 businesses and 72 storefronts. Beverly Road forms a second commercial strip on the north side, and the Red Line light rail stops at Mt. Lebanon Station beneath Uptown, running through the Mt. Lebanon Tunnel toward the city.

Named neighborhoods include Virginia Manor, Hoodridge, Mission Hills, Seminole Hills, Beverly Heights and Washington Park. The Mt. Lebanon School District is a walking district with no school bus service, and fifteen parks cover about 200 acres.

Cash works best when the closing date or the property's shape matters more than a retail price. A cash buyer purchases as is, so repairs and permit clean-up fall into the buyer's own plan. Typical situations include:

  • An inherited house with older systems that no one in the family wants to renovate.
  • A property with unfinished or unpermitted work that would take weeks of Inspection Office review.
  • A tenant-occupied house where the owner wants out of landlord duties.
  • A move on a short timeline, such as a job change that leaves two mortgages.

Whoever buys, ask the Inspection Office whether any permit is open before agreeing on a closing date, since municipal lien letters are part of the paperwork.

faqs.q: Does Mt. Lebanon require a resale inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: The Certificate of Occupancy covers changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction, not an ordinary resale. Lien letters are withheld while permits are open, so close those out first and call the Inspection Office at 412-343-3408 about your address.

faqs.q: When are Mt. Lebanon property taxes due?
faqs.a: Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount through July 31, face value from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty afterward. School tax can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28.

faqs.q: What starts an Allegheny County assessment appeal for a Mt. Lebanon home?
faqs.a: File with the county's Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review during the annual window, July 1 through September 1. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal, because the board applies the county common level ratio to market value.

faqs.q: What does the realty transfer tax cost on a Mt. Lebanon sale?
faqs.a: The state charges 1 percent and local municipal and school shares come on top, so the countywide total ranges from 2 to 5 percent. Ask the county Department of Real Estate for the figure that applies to Mt. Lebanon.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Mt. Lebanon house that has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, but work done without a permit can lead to fines set by the magisterial district judge. Ask the Inspection Office how to bring it into compliance, or discuss an as-is sale with a buyer who will take the house as it is.
